feedback: If a learner filters salty water and evaporating a few drops of the filtrate leaves salt behind: the salt is dissolved, not a suspended solid, and filter paper only holds back undissolved bits. Reconnect to dissolving, then ask which part is wanted: evaporation/crystallisation to recover the salt, or distillation to recover the water.

If a learner evaporates salty water when the WATER was wanted: ask 'which part do we want to keep?' Evaporation keeps the salt and loses the water as vapour; to keep the water you must condense it — distillation.

If a learner picks a method by memory of a past practical: prompt 'what is different about the things you're separating — dissolved? insoluble? different boiling points? different colours?' so the property drives the choice.

On the chromatogram: if the black spot splits into three colours at different heights, that shows the 'one' ink was a mixture of at least three dyes, each with a different attraction to paper versus solvent, so they travel different distances.
After a mismatched technique visibly fails, point back to the property difference that the correct method exploits rather than supplying the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Each technique exploits a specific property difference, so the method must be selected from the mixture's properties and from which component you want to keep — not recalled from a past practical. Distillation keeps the liquid (condensed and collected pure); evaporation/crystallisation keeps the solid. Chromatography shows at least how many substances are present.
learnerActions: Work from a mixture bank: muddy/sandy water, salty water, rock salt, a spot of black felt-tip ink.
For each mixture, first state the property difference between its components (insoluble solid? dissolved solid? liquids of different boiling point? different coloured dyes?) BEFORE choosing a method.
Choose and set up one of four stations — filtration, crystallisation/evaporation, distillation, chromatography — and run it.

At filtration: pour muddy water through filter paper. Watch a clearer filtrate drip through while insoluble mud/sand stays on the paper. Note that very fine particles can leave it slightly cloudy and that anything dissolved passes through, so the filtrate is not pure water.
At crystallisation/evaporation: heat salty water and watch white salt left behind as the water leaves.

At distillation: watch the solvent boil up, travel into the cooled condenser, turn back to liquid and drip out as pure liquid while the salt stays in the flask — trace the one flow heat→evaporate→condense→collect.

At chromatography: place an ink spot on a pencil start line near the bottom of the paper. Stand the paper in solvent kept BELOW the spot so the dye climbs the paper rather than washing straight into the solvent. Watch whether the black dot climbs and splits into separate coloured spots; many black inks do, but not all. Count the spots to give the minimum number of dyes present.

Tackle a multi-component mixture (e.g. rock salt treated as salt + insoluble rock/sand: dissolve in water, filter off the insoluble rock/sand, then recover the salt) that requires an ordered sequence of techniques.

Deliberately try a mismatched technique (e.g. filtering salty water). Show that it fails by evaporating a few drops of the filtrate: white salt is left behind, so the salt went through the paper. Then revise the choice using the property.
activities.title: Separation lab: choose, run, and check the technique

feedback: For a match error, point back to the property difference (insoluble solid → filter; dissolved solid → crystallise/evaporate; liquids by boiling point → distil; coloured dyes → chromatography).
For a sequencing error, ask which component must be removed first and why (e.g. remove insoluble sand by filtration before recovering dissolved salt).
When reading the chromatogram, confirm that more separate spots means at least that many substances and that a higher spot was more strongly attracted to the solvent relative to the paper.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners consolidate technique selection, step sequencing, and chromatogram interpretation, including that the number of spots shows the minimum number of substances.
learnerActions: Match each described mixture to the technique that exploits the right property difference.
Put the steps of a multi-technique separation (e.g. salt + insoluble sand in water) into a working order.

Read a given chromatogram: state how many components are present and which travelled furthest, and, where distances are provided, compute or compare Rf values (distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent front).
Explain in one line why filtration removes sand from water but not dissolved salt.
activities.title: Match, sequence, and read a chromatogram

feedback: If the distillate still seems impure, discuss setup issues (collection timing, contamination) rather than concluding the method fails.
Compare what was expected from the property-based reasoning with what was observed.
activities.intendedInsight: Real practicals give direct experience of assembling apparatus, handling real materials, and observing genuine outcomes, reinforcing that method choice is justified by what actually separates.
learnerActions: Carry out a real filtration of muddy water and inspect the filtrate.

Set up a real distillation of salty water and collect the distillate. Test whether the distillate is free of salt by evaporating a few drops on a clean watch glass and checking for any white residue. Appearance can't show this, because salty water also looks clear, and salt left in the flask says nothing about the distillate. Never taste substances in the lab.
Run paper chromatography on a felt-tip ink spot, keeping the solvent level below the spot, and count the separated colours.
Where safe apparatus and supervision allow, assemble the distillation apparatus so the physical connections (flask, condenser, collection vessel) are handled directly.
activities.title: Real separation practicals (hands-on complement)
